rationale: B wins because it is cleaner on the one thing this assignment cannot forgive: factual control. Its first angle says "Duolingo says beta users talked to its AI character for nine minutes at a stretch," while A opens with "talking to its cartoon owl" even though the update names Lily. A is sharper on proof in places, but cute wrongness is still wrongness, and journalists do not grade on charm.
gaps_in_A: "talking to its cartoon owl" misidentifies the feature; the update says users talk with Lily, not the owl. Cute headline, bad fact-check.
"its most-criticized design" inflates "some educators have publicly criticized gamification" into a superlative the facts do not support.
"the beta number is being published for the first time" is not in the supplied update. Ask whether it is first public; do not assert it.
"expensive AI feature" and the aside about "existing music or math courses" drag in unproven context. Even caveated, it makes the set look like it is leaning on memory instead of the brief.
gaps_in_B: "Critics called Duolingo shallow" overstates the update; the fact supplied is that some educators criticized gamification as shallow learning.
"the first public engagement figure" is asserted without support. Same sin as A, just better dressed.
"consumer-AI reporter... AI companions" borrows a beat the update does not quite earn. The facts support voice agents in learning apps, not the AI-companion boom.
"A chess or board-games reporter" is specific, but the angle is thin. Without course depth, designer, play mode, or chess-community stakes, it is launch filler with a better address label.
